title: Physics Motivation and DarkSHINE Experiment
body:
01 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Physics Motivation and
DarkSHINE Experiment

Light dark matter and an accelerator-based missing-energy search
notes: Gravitational observations give us evidence for dark matter. To search for it in the laboratory, we need a model of how it interacts with ordinary matter.

title: Evidence for dark matter
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Evidence for dark matter

Extended mass distributions

Orbital velocities remain high beyond the luminous disc.

Mass and gas separate

Lensing traces gravitating matter beyond the hot gas.

A non-baryonic component

The matter budget is constrained across cosmic scales.

These observations constrain the abundance and distribution of dark matter; its particle identity remains unknown.
Clowe et al., ApJ 648 (2006) L109; Planck 2018.
notes:
We see evidence for dark matter on very different scales.

The rotation curves indicate an extended mass distribution beyond the visible stellar disc.

In the Bullet Cluster, the hot gas and the mass inferred from gravitational lensing are spatially separated after the collision.

CMB (cosmic microwave background) observations require a substantial non-baryonic matter component.

Together, these observations constrain dark matter's abundance and distribution.
source: Clowe et al., ApJ 648 (2006) L109; Planck 2018. Image: supplied reference assets.

title: What observations constrain
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# What observations constrain

Observational requirements

Long-lived on cosmological time scales.

Sufficiently cold to form the observed structures.

Model-dependent bounds

Statistics, thermal history and late energy injection determine the relevant limits.
notes:
However, the particle identity of dark matter and its coupling to ordinary matter remain unknown.

The candidate masses span about 10⁻²¹ eV to PeV. Ultralight candidates behave as coherent fields; their wavelength must fit inside the galactic halos we observe. For heavier particle candidates, the relic abundance depends on how they were produced. WIMPs freeze out from thermal equilibrium when annihilation becomes too slow. Freeze-in candidates are produced through interactions too weak to establish equilibrium.

title: Complementary dark-matter searches
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Complementary dark-matter searches
DarkSHINE probes controlled production through missing energy and momentum.
notes: Direct detection looks for interactions of Galactic dark matter in a detector. It becomes difficult when the recoil energy is very small. Indirect detection looks for products of dark-matter annihilation or decay. At an accelerator, we try to produce dark matter in collision.

notes: This lagrangian describes kinetic mixing between the photon and the dark photon. The parameter epsilon gives the dark photon a small coupling to the electromagnetic current. Its mass determines the kinematics, and epsilon squared approximately scales the production rate. We assume that the dark photon can decay to lighter dark-sector particles, with an invisible decay branching ratio close to 1.

8 GeVDesign beam energy

A dedicated extraction branch provides the basis for the electron programme. Positron delivery is a prospective extension.
notes: We will have high-repetition-rate electron beam delivered by SHINE (Shanghai High Repetition-Rate XFEL and Extreme Light Facility). We take an electron-beam design energy of 8 GeV and a design repetition rate of 1 MHz as inputs to the DarkSHINE conceptual design. We have a dedicated electron extraction branch alongside the free-electron-laser beamlines. The benchmark count is three times ten to the fourteen incident electrons, expressed as EOT (electrons on target).

title: DarkSHINE detector conceptual design Baseline 1
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# DarkSHINE detector conceptual design Baseline 1
notes: This is the DarkSHINE detector design in the Baseline 1 configuration. Following the beam, the tagging tracker measures the incident electron momentum in the magnetic field. The electron crosses a thin tungsten target, and the recoil tracker measures the outgoing charged particle. The ECAL measures electromagnetic energy and its spatial distribution. The larger HCAL detects hadrons and penetrating muons for background rejection. The trackers use silicon strips, while the ECAL is a segmented LYSO crystal array.

title: Detector requirements for a missing-energy search
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Detector requirements for a missing-energy search
SubsystemRequirement / benchmark
Tagging trackerHit resolution ; momentum resolution at 8 GeV
Tungsten target; limit multiple scattering
Recoil trackerAccept recoils from to 2 GeV; hit resolution
LYSO ECALHigh granularity; precise e/γ energy measurement
Fe/scintillator HCALNeutron veto inefficiency for ; at lower energies
notes: The detector requirements follow from the missing-energy measurement. The tagging tracker needs a hit precision below 10 micrometres and a momentum resolution below 2 percent at 8 GeV. The tungsten target is 0.1 radiation lengths thick to limit multiple scattering. The recoil tracker needs to measure charged particles from about 30 MeV to 2 GeV. The ECAL needs high granularity and precise energy measurement to resolve localised electromagnetic deposits. The HCAL requirements are driven by the neutron background: veto inefficiency below ten to the minus five above roughly 2 GeV, and below ten to the minus three at lower energies.

title: Electron-mode signal and background rejection
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Electron-mode signal and background rejection
SignalElectron beam

One soft recoil electron with substantial missing energy and momentum.

SelectionVisible vetoes

Measurements used together

  • Exactly one incident particle
  • A recoil carrying less momentum
  • Low electromagnetic energy
  • No significant hadronic or muon activity

Hard bremsstrahlung is abundant. Rare photonuclear, electronuclear and muon-pair processes can leave poorly measured energy.

The sensitivity is controlled by the rare surviving tails of Standard Model interactions.
notes: In electron mode, dark bremsstrahlung produces a dark photon that decays invisibly, together with a recoil electron carrying only part of the beam energy. Ordinary bremsstrahlung can also leave a soft electron, but the photon normally deposits its energy in the ECAL. Rare photonuclear and muon-pair processes can transfer that energy to hadrons or muons, or send it outside the detector acceptance. We combine the measured momentum, electromagnetic energy and HCAL veto to reject these events.
source: J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023).

title: Standard Model background hierarchy
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Standard Model background hierarchy

Hard-photon branches

: identified by tracker and ECAL.

Photonuclear / : hadrons and muons.

Different rejection mechanisms

Electronuclear produces hadrons. HCAL vetoes hadronic and muonic activity.

Residual background

Muon pairs are effectively rejected by HCAL. PN / EN tails require extrapolation into the signal region.

J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023); Baseline Design Report, arXiv:2411.09345.
notes:
Most beam electrons pass through the thin target with bremstrulung process. Hard bremsstrahlung produces a recoil electron and an energetic photon. The rarer photonuclear and muon-pair branches put energy into hadrons or muons, making the HCAL veto essential.

Muon pairs are effectively rejected by HCAL. The surviving PN and EN tails determine the main background in the signal region.
source: J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023), Secs. 4.2, 5 and 6.1; Fig. 8 and Table 2.

title: Event Simulation and Reconstruction in DarkSHINE
body:
02 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Event Simulation and
Reconstruction in DarkSHINE

A configurable chain for detector studies and rare-process production
notes: I will now describe our work on the simulation framework, from defining the detector and recording events to reducing the time needed to simulate rare backgrounds.

title: The DarkSHINE software framework
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# The DarkSHINE software framework
From a beam particle to an analysis sample
8 GeV e⁻ beam
My contributions: General design of software framework, DSimu, DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, and ACTS integration.
notes:
Generation defines the beam or signal process. DSimu simulates the detector interactions with Geant4, DEvent stores truth and hit collections, and DAna performs digitisation and reconstruction. DDis displays individual events, and the analysis uses the reconstructed observables to select events and calculate limits.

The four plots show recoil kinematics from the 8 GeV CDR electron-mode simulation. Signal electrons have lower energies than the background concentrated near the beam energy. Transverse momentum provides further discrimination; that panel selects recoil energies between 50 MeV and 4 GeV. The recoil angle and transverse separation describe how the signal spreads across the tracking detector and how that spread changes with dark-photon mass.

My contributions are the general framework design, DSimu, DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, and ACTS integration.
source: DSS software framework; X. Zhu, Nucl. Part. Phys. Proc. 346 (2024) 57.

title: A common event model: DEvent
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# A common event model: DEvent
What a stored event lets us study
Truth particles + stepsMomentum, energy, origin, endpoint and ancestryTrace the interaction that produced a background
Simulated hitsDeposited energy, position, time and cell IDStudy shower topology and detector response
Response + reconstructed objectsCell signals, fitted tracks and clustersBuild visible energy, recoil momentum and vetoes
One event, linked views

Follow the particle history into detector deposits, then compare with reconstructed tracks and calorimeter response.
notes: DEvent carries several views of the same physical event. Truth particles and steps record momenta, energies, origins and interaction history. Simulated hits record deposited energy, positions, times and detector cell identifiers. Detector-response collections and reconstructed objects provide cell signals, fitted tracks and clusters. The event display shows the link between a particle trajectory and the shower it produces. For a background entering the signal region, we can trace its origin, inspect veto activity and identify missed tracks or clusters. Stored particle and hit records also let us rerun digitisation and reconstruction.

title: Geometry navigation and event-record optimisation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Geometry navigation and event-record optimisation
Store the quantities needed for physics

Smaller records, explicit content

InformationStored quantities / change
Particle kinematicspₓ, pᵧ, p_z, E, m → float
Origin and trajectoryVertex and endpoint x, y, z → float
Detector hitsEnergy, time, x, y, z → float; compact cell IDs
Remove duplicationCalculate |p| from components; identify particles by PDG ID
Step historyRecord primary-electron steps in the tracker region
60.1 → 13.7 KB/eventEvent-record benchmark
Navigate a finely segmented detector

Bounding volume hierarchy

Nested bounding volumes reduce volume checks at each Geant4 step.

260 → 42 ms/eventNavigation benchmark
notes:
We optimised the event records and Geant4 geometry navigation for large simulation samples. Particle records store momentum components, energy, mass, production vertices and endpoints. Hits store deposited energy, time, position and cell identifiers. We use float precision for these fields and remove duplicated quantities: momentum magnitude is calculated from its components, and PDG identifiers replace repeated particle-name strings. The event-record benchmark stores primary-electron step histories in the tracker region. These changes reduce the event size from about sixty to fourteen kilobytes.

A bounding volume hierarchy reduces the number of individual detector volumes checked at each Geant4 step. The navigation benchmark improves from about a quarter of a second to forty milliseconds per event.

title: Generator-level filtering with staged Geant4 tracking
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Generator-level filtering with staged Geant4 tracking
Primary interaction

Was enough energy transferred?

Check the primary energy loss and, when requested, a hard bremsstrahlung photon.

Rare secondary process

Did the required interaction occur?

Select process or particle type, longitudinal region and energy interval.

Visible shower energy

Can this event still pass?

Stop once accumulated truth ECAL energy exceeds the production bound.
notes: The filter follows the physics of rare backgrounds. At stage zero, we track the primary particle and defer its secondaries. We inspect the primary energy loss and can require a hard bremsstrahlung photon. At stage one, we release secondaries from the selected longitudinal region. The process filter selects a photonuclear, electronuclear or muon-pair interaction and its energy transfer. The particle filter selects the secondary species and energy. Events passing these conditions proceed to stage two, where the remaining tracks are released. The ECAL veto stops an event as soon as its accumulated deposited energy exceeds the production bound.

title: Rare-process biasing and physical normalisation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Rare-process biasing and physical normalisation
01 | Enrich the physics of interest

Choose process, material and energy

  • PN, EN or muon-pair production in the target / ECAL
  • Increase the selected interaction cross section above an energy threshold
  • Simulate secondary interactions, energy deposits and leakage
02 | Measure the rate dependence on bias
Eligible beam events × physical interaction probability
Enrich rare final states for detector studies; recover their rate from the production normalisation.
notes:
Biasing increases the statistics for rare photonuclear, electronuclear and muon-pair final states. We select the process, material region and energy threshold, then enhance its interaction cross section. Geant4 simulates the secondary interactions, energy deposits and leakage.

The ECAL muon-pair scan shows the interaction probability increasing with the bias factor and eventually saturating. We fit this dependence and evaluate the physical probability at bias factor one. Multiplying by the fraction of beam events containing an eligible particle gives the process rate per incident particle, which sets the expected event count at a given EOT or POT.

title: Parallel event simulation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Parallel event simulation
Independent beam events

One physics chain per worker

Each worker runs generation, particle tracking in Geant4 and event filling with its own random and event state.

Particles + ancestryTracker hitsECAL / HCAL deposits

Merge the same named collections for reconstruction and analysis.

10⁶ events, eight concurrent units:
8-thread job: 15,328 s
8 single-thread jobs: 16,648 s
notes:
Beam events are independent, so each worker runs a complete event: primary generation, Geant4 particle tracking and event filling. This required worker-local event storage, random-number handling and changes to shared framework state. The particle and detector-hit collections from the workers are merged for reconstruction and analysis.

The plot shows throughput increasing with worker count. For one million events and eight concurrent units, one eight-thread job takes about 4.3 hours, compared with about 4.6 hours for eight single-thread jobs.

title: Optical response with a lookup table
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Optical response with a lookup table
Replace repeated photon propagation

Predict detected light and arrival time

Tabulate response versus emission position and direction.

Detection probabilityPhoton transit time

Sample this response for scintillation photons during shower simulation.

~200 → ~4 s/eventFull optical tracking → LUT

Collected light versus emission depth and angle.

Arrival-time response of the detected photons.

Validate the light yield and time response; the tested detection efficiencies agree within 5%.
Credit: Qibin Liu
notes:
The lookup table replaces repeated optical-photon propagation. It is indexed by emission position and direction and provides the detection probability and photon transit-time distribution. These determine the collected light and its arrival time at the sensor.

The detection-efficiency comparison with full optical tracking agrees within five percent over the tested depth and angle range. The right plot compares the transit-time spectra. The complete-event runtime decreases from about 200 seconds to four seconds. This optical-response work was contributed by Qibin Liu.

title: Digitisation connects deposits to observables
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Digitisation connects deposits to observables
Physics response model

From photons to cell energy

SiPM saturation and recovery, electronic noise, finite dynamic range and ADC sampling.

Pulse amplitude / integralCell energyTiming

Cell energies feed the ECAL total-energy and maximum-cell selections.

Credit: Qibin Liu
notes: Digitisation converts simulated deposits into measurable signals. After scintillation and light collection, each detected photon contributes a single-photoelectron pulse. Summing these pulses in time gives the cell waveform. The model includes SiPM saturation and recovery, electronic noise, finite dynamic range and ADC sampling. Calibration converts the pulse response into cell energy. Summing the cells gives the ECAL total energy, while the largest cell energy defines the maximum-cell observable. These studies were contributed by Qibin Liu.

title: Track finding and fitting
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Track finding and fitting
From strip measurements to a momentum estimate
01 | Find the track

Associate hits across layers; rank circle candidates and remove accepted hits.

02 | Fit the trajectory

Propagate through the field and material with measurement errors, energy loss and multiple scattering.

03 | Evaluate tracking performance

Momentum resolution versus beam energy and layer count constrains the recoil measurement.

DarkSHINE Collaboration, Baseline Design Report, arXiv:2411.09345
notes:
Track finding associates strip measurements with a common trajectory. The finder ranks circle candidates and removes accepted hits before continuing. Track fitting estimates momentum and covariance using the magnetic field, material, measurement errors, energy loss and multiple scattering.

The CDR plot shows relative momentum resolution versus beam energy for four to ten recoil-tracker layers. Multiple scattering worsens the resolution at low energies; small curvature and the available lever arm limit it at high energies. Six layers provide the Baseline 1 balance between tracking performance and material. The reconstructed momentum and track multiplicity enter the missing-momentum selection.
source: DarkSHINE Baseline Design Report, arXiv:2411.09345; CDR TrackerMomentumReso.pdf.

title: ACTS integration in DarkSHINE
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# ACTS integration in DarkSHINE
Reconstruction interfaces
Example output: track-parameter pull
Fit residual relative to its estimated uncertainty
ACTS provides fitted states and covariance, vertex candidates, and track extrapolation to ECAL.
My contributions: ACTS sequencer, geometry/field adapters and reconstruction interfaces.
notes:
We convert the detector geometry into ACTS surfaces and strip-pair hits into measurements and source links. The sequencer runs truth-smeared seeding, combinatorial Kalman finding, track conversion and vertex reconstruction. Fitted tracks are extrapolated to the ECAL to provide impact positions.

The 2023 truth-assisted fitter test shows the track-parameter pull versus transverse momentum. The pull is the fitted-minus-truth residual divided by its estimated uncertainty. The distribution is concentrated near zero. My contributions are the ACTS sequencer and the geometry, magnetic-field and reconstruction interfaces.
source: Candidate contribution: ACTS sequencer, geometry/field adapters and reconstruction interfaces.

title: Positron-Beam-Mode Analysis
body:
03 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Positron-Beam-Mode
Analysis

Three production mechanisms, three exclusive reconstructed categories
notes: The positron study uses the Baseline 1 detector. I will introduce its additional production mechanisms, event selection and expected sensitivity.

title: Why a positron beam?
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Why a positron beam?
for an 8 GeV beam and an electron initially at rest.
notes: A positron can undergo dark bremsstrahlung and annihilate with an atomic electron. Non-resonant annihilation produces a photon and a dark photon. Resonant annihilation produces a dark photon that decays to a dark-matter pair, with no accompanying hard visible particle. For an electron initially at rest, an 8 GeV positron gives a centre-of-mass energy of about ninety MeV. This sets the characteristic mass scale for annihilation production.

title: Production mechanisms at 8 GeV
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Production mechanisms at 8 GeV
Annihilation kinematics

Annihilation adds a mass scale

For an electron at rest,

Off-shell dark-photon exchange extends the annihilation contribution above this mass scale.

The radiative endpoint and resonant enhancement motivate a detector-level comparison near 90 MeV.
X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900.
notes: Nuclear bremsstrahlung covers a broad range of mediator masses. Non-resonant annihilation is limited by the available centre-of-mass energy, and resonant production is enhanced near that energy. An 8 GeV positron annihilating with an electron at rest has a centre-of-mass energy of about ninety MeV. Off-shell dark-photon exchange extends the annihilation contribution above this mass scale.
source: X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900. Original cross-section plot.

title: Signal and background samples
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal and background samples
Efficiency samples

Signal grid

MechanismMass points
Dark bremsstrahlung30
Non-resonant annihilation18
Resonant annihilation23

events per channel–mass point.

CalcHEP kinematics followed by Geant4 detector simulation.

Background predictions

Background production

  • PN, EN and muon-pair conversion
  • Target/tracker and ECAL locations
  • Additional target-annihilation sample
  • Independent inclusive sample: POT

Common benchmark: 8 GeV, POT, baseline 1 detector.

Equal generated signal counts measure efficiency. Cross sections determine the physical mixture.
arXiv:2609.05900
notes:
We simulate 30 bremsstrahlung mass points, 18 non-resonant points and 23 resonant points, with a hundred thousand events at each channel–mass point. CalcHEP provides the signal kinematics, followed by Geant4 detector simulation. These samples determine the selection efficiencies; cross sections set the relative production rates.

Dedicated background samples cover photonuclear, positron-nuclear and muon-pair processes in the target or tracker and in the ECAL, plus ordinary target annihilation. The positron-nuclear sample uses the EN label. An independent inclusive sample contains 2.5 billion POT for background validation. The sensitivity benchmark is 8 GeV, 3 × 10¹⁴ POT and Baseline 1.

# Three exclusive signal regions
SelectionSR1: recoil positronSR2: photon-likeSR3: low activity
Tagging tracks= 1= 1= 1

Missing momentum> 4 GeV——
ECAL total energy< 2.5 GeV< 2 GeV< 2 GeV

HCAL total energy< 100 MeV< 100 MeV< 100 MeV
HCAL maximum cell< 1 MeV< 1 MeV< 1 MeV
Track multiplicity separates SR1. Complementary ECAL maximum-cell cuts separate SR2 and SR3.
notes: Every signal region requires exactly one tagging track. SR1 requires one recoil track, missing momentum above 4 GeV and total ECAL energy below 2.5 GeV. SR2 and SR3 require no recoil track and total ECAL energy below 2 GeV. A maximum-cell energy of at least 1 MeV defines SR2; below 1 MeV defines SR3. All three regions require HCAL total energy below 100 MeV and maximum-cell energy below 1 MeV. These selections form three exclusive categories.

title: Momentum and total-energy discrimination
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Momentum and total-energy discrimination
The production filter requires missing momentum > 1 GeV. The final SR1 requirement is > 4 GeV.
arXiv:2609.05900
notes: The missing-momentum distribution separates soft-recoil signal events from background. The background sample passes a loose production filter at 1 GeV; the final SR1 selection requires more than 4 GeV. For non-resonant annihilation, the accompanying photon becomes soft near the mediator-mass endpoint. This produces the low total-ECAL-energy signal distribution near 90 MeV.

title: Maximum-cell energy separates the zero-track sample
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Maximum-cell energy separates the zero-track sample
defines SR2; defines SR3.
notes: For events with no recoil track, the largest ECAL cell distinguishes a photon deposit from a nearly empty calorimeter. The non-resonant distribution changes with mediator mass because the accompanying photon kinematics change. Resonant annihilation usually leaves little activity, with some deposits from interactions in the tracker material. A maximum-cell energy of at least 1 MeV selects SR2; below 1 MeV selects SR3.

title: Signal efficiency across the mass scan
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal efficiency across the mass scan
All nine channel-to-region efficiencies enter the signal prediction.
notes:
These curves show the cutflow efficiencies for each production mechanism in its primary signal region, normalised to the generated sample. We combine the efficiencies with production cross sections to predict the signal yields.

Track reconstruction and photon detection can move events between regions. A missed recoil track can put a bremsstrahlung event into a zero-track category; a soft or undetected photon can put a non-resonant event into the low-activity category. All nine channel-to-region efficiencies enter the signal prediction.

title: Signal migration at 90 MeV
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal migration at 90 MeV
||
At 90 MeV, non-resonant annihilation supplies about 95% of SR2; resonant annihilation supplies about 84% of SR3.
notes: At a mediator mass of 90 MeV, epsilon squared of 10⁻¹² and 3 × 10¹⁴ POT, the matrix gives the expected selected event counts. Non-resonant annihilation supplies about 95 percent of SR2, and resonant annihilation supplies about 84 percent of SR3. Bremsstrahlung contributes very little at this mass. The off-diagonal entries show migration between the production mechanisms' primary regions.

title: Background rejection in the available simulation
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Background rejection in the available simulation
PN ECAL | cumulative unweighted simulated counts
No simulated events survive the full selection; the residual background is estimated by extrapolation.
notes: This cutflow shows cumulative simulated counts for photonuclear interactions in the ECAL. The recoil-track requirement separates the one-track and zero-track categories. SR1 then requires missing momentum above 4 GeV. SR2 requires an ECAL maximum-cell energy of at least 1 MeV, while SR3 requires total ECAL energy below 2 GeV. All three regions apply the HCAL total-energy and maximum-cell vetoes. The last step requires ECAL total energy below 2.5 GeV in SR1, below 2 GeV in SR2, and maximum-cell energy below 1 MeV in SR3. No simulated events survive the full selection. We estimate the residual background by extrapolating the survival distributions.

Rate validation

Dedicated samples are normalised using process rates and filter acceptance.

The inclusive sample tests the populated survival trend.

notes: We normalise each dedicated sample to its equivalent unbiased POT using the generation attempts, generator acceptance and physical branching ratio. The plot compares the sum of these normalised samples, including target annihilation, with the independent inclusive sample. Their survival trends agree in the populated sidebands, validating the dedicated-sample normalisation used for background estimation.

RegionExtrapolation methodNominal events

Background yields are extrapolated from populated sidebands to the final selection thresholds.
notes: For SR1 and SR2, we fit the dedicated survival curves with a power law in the total-ECAL-energy threshold. SR3 uses a two-dimensional fit to account for the correlation between total energy and maximum-cell energy. Summing the process contributions gives about three hundredths of an event in SR1, and of order ten to the minus four events in each zero-track region. These fits extrapolate the populated sidebands to the final selection thresholds.

title: Combined statistical interpretation
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Combined statistical interpretation
01Build the signal prediction
02Fit exclusive regions

Joint region model

  • Three mutually exclusive signal regions
  • One signal strength for all mechanisms
  • Include all channel-to-region migrations
  • Profile nuisance parameters in the fit
03Expected limit

Expected 90% CL limits

Background-only expectation using and asymptotic profile likelihood.

Background-shape uncertainties are uncorrelated between bins in the reported construction.

arXiv:2609.05900
notes: At each mass, we sum all three production mechanisms in every signal region, including migration. A common signal-strength parameter scales their rates through the kinetic mixing. We combine the three exclusive regions in a binned profile likelihood and profile the nuisance parameters. The expected 90 percent confidence-level limit uses CLs and the asymptotic profile likelihood under the background-only hypothesis. Background-shape uncertainties are uncorrelated between bins.

title: Annihilation drives the gain near 90 MeV
body:

# Annihilation drives the gain near 90 MeV
Mechanism comparison

Non-resonant annihilation gives the strongest individual projected limit at this mass.
notes: Each individual curve keeps 1 production mechanism but uses all 3 regions and the same background model. It therefore includes migration between regions. At 90 MeV, non-resonant annihilation gives the strongest individual expected limit, roughly seven times ten to the minus thirteen in epsilon squared. Resonant annihilation also contributes, and the combined limit is about five times ten to the minus thirteen. Much of the gain comes from non-resonant annihilation near the radiative endpoint, where the accompanying photon can pass the selection.

body:

8 GeV, baseline 1

title: Positron study: results and refinements
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Positron study: results and refinements
Completed analysis

Accomplished in this study

  • Detector-level efficiencies for three production mechanisms
  • Three exclusive regions and all channel-to-region migrations
  • Dedicated background predictions and an inclusive cross-check
  • Combined 90% CL sensitivity at the 8 GeV benchmark
Further refinements

Opportunities to improve

  • Detector-response inputs informed by measurements
  • Efficient sampling of rare background tails
  • Extended uncertainty models for new configurations
notes:
The positron analysis evaluates three production mechanisms in every reconstructed category, includes migration, estimates the background and combines the three exclusive regions. It finds a sensitivity gain from annihilation, especially near 90 MeV.

Further studies can use detector measurements to refine response inputs, increase rare-background statistics and extend the uncertainty models for new detector and beam configurations.

title: Main results

Summary and outlook
# Main results
My software contributions

Framework design and implementation

  • General framework design; simulation software (DSimu) and event model (DEvent)
  • Rare-process biasing, staged filtering and production optimisation
  • ACTS integration for tracking and ECAL extrapolation
Positron-beam analysis

Combined positron sensitivity

Three production mechanisms, full detector simulation and three exclusive signal regions, including all channel-to-region migrations.

90% CL expected limit at 90 MeV
POT, 8 GeV, Baseline 1

Annihilation improves the projected reach near 90 MeV by about two orders of magnitude.
notes:
My software contributions cover the general framework design, the development of DSimu and DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, production optimisation, and ACTS integration. Together with the collaboration's response and reconstruction work, these components connect simulated interactions to the observables used in the physics analysis.

I used this framework to complete a detector-level positron-beam study with three production mechanisms and three exclusive signal regions. The signal calculation includes migration between all channel and region combinations. Combining the regions gives an expected 90 percent confidence-level limit of about five times ten to the minus thirteen in epsilon squared at a mediator mass of 90 MeV and three times ten to the fourteen POT. At the same detector benchmark and matching integrated luminosity, annihilation improves the reach near this mass by about two orders of magnitude relative to the earlier electron-beam projection.

title: Outlook
body:
Summary and outlook
# Outlook
Detector response

Tune digitisation, calibration and veto selections with prototype and beam-test measurements.

Rare-process simulation

Increase dedicated background statistics with improved sampling and more detailed uncertainty models.

Positron beam energies

Extend the analysis to additional design energies and optimise selections for each mass range.

Changing the positron beam energy shifts the annihilation mass range.
notes:
Prototype and beam-test measurements can tune digitisation, calibration and veto selections. Improved rare-process sampling can increase background statistics and support more detailed uncertainty models.

Varying the positron beam energy shifts the characteristic annihilation mass as the square root of the beam energy. Additional beam energies can probe other mediator masses, with selections optimised for their recoil and photon kinematics.
